title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on U.S. Gulf Coast as Category 2 storm

image.caption: An American flag is seen flapping in the wind on Alabama's Mon Louis Island ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias on Friday. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Hurricane Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surge.
U.S. National Hurricane Center says Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., on Friday

The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Fla., the Miami-based U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 169 km/h. The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore.

"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard "throughout the region."

Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white sand beaches that are dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks. Forecasters warned the conditions could also stir up tornadoes.
People are seen leaving a gas station in Mobile, Ala., on Friday, which had been boarded up prior to the hurricane's arrival. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)
In Mobile, Ala., officials reported downed trees and power lines, while Emerald Coast Utilities Authority, which serves parts of Florida, issued a boil-water notice for its customers.
More than 400,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power Friday evening, according to poweroutage.com.
Residents in Panama City, Fla., braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.
"I mean, it's just the nature of the beast. It's Florida," said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.
A downed tree blocks a road in Pensacola, Fla., on Friday, as Isaias-driven wind and rain approached the area. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 1.8 to 2.7 metres, according to the hurricane centre. Places most at risk include Florida's Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.

Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighbourhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters and picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile.
"Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good," she said. "It's just another adventure."

Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Ala., imposed a curfew beginning Friday evening until morning.
Dozens of Waffle Houses closed

In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm's severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida-native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.

"We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it's not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed," said Frazier. "Which is a pretty big deal."
DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.
The state's National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search and rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.
